claim: Natural environments of living organisms are often dynamic and multifactorial, with multiple parameters fluctuating over time.
source: Natural environments of living organisms are often dynamic and multifactorial, with multiple parameters fluctuating over time.
evidence: This is a general statement about natural environments presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this study.

claim: Cell proliferation depends on the phasing of periodic osmotic stress and glucose deprivation.
source: Strikingly, we observed that cell proliferation, survival, and signaling depend on the phasing of the two periodic stresses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of division rates under different phasing conditions shown in the manuscript.

claim: Cells divided faster when fluctuations of hyperosmotic stress and glucose deprivation occurred in phase than when the two stresses occurred alternatively.
source: Cells divided faster, survived longer, and showed decreased transcriptional response when fluctuations of hyperosmotic stress and glucose deprivation occurred in phase than when the two stresses occurred alternatively.
evidence: This is directly supported by division rate measurements comparing IPS and AS conditions presented in Figure 3.

claim: Cells survived longer when fluctuations of hyperosmotic stress and glucose deprivation occurred in phase than when the two stresses occurred alternatively.
source: Cells divided faster, survived longer, and showed decreased transcriptional response when fluctuations of hyperosmotic stress and glucose deprivation occurred in phase than when the two stresses occurred alternatively.
evidence: This is supported by death rate measurements comparing IPS and AS conditions presented in Figure 5.

claim: Cells showed decreased transcriptional response when fluctuations of hyperosmotic stress and glucose deprivation occurred in phase than when the two stresses occurred alternatively.
source: Cells divided faster, survived longer, and showed decreased transcriptional response when fluctuations of hyperosmotic stress and glucose deprivation occurred in phase than when the two stresses occurred alternatively.
evidence: This is supported by PSTL1-mCitrine expression measurements comparing IPS and AS conditions presented in Figure 7.

claim: Glucose availability regulates yeast responses to dynamic osmotic stress.
source: Therefore, glucose availability regulates yeast responses to dynamic osmotic stress, showcasing the key role of metabolic fluctuations in cellular responses to dynamic stress.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the differential responses observed under IPS vs AS conditions throughout the study.

claim: Mutants with impaired osmotic stress response were better adapted to alternating stresses than wild-type cells.
source: We also found that mutants with impaired osmotic stress response were better adapted to alternating stresses than wild-type cells, showing that genetic mechanisms of adaptation to a persistent stress factor can be detrimental under dynamically interacting conditions.
evidence: This is supported by population growth rate measurements of HOG pathway mutants under AS conditions shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Genetic mechanisms of adaptation to a persistent stress factor can be detrimental under dynamically interacting conditions.
source: We also found that mutants with impaired osmotic stress response were better adapted to alternating stresses than wild-type cells, showing that genetic mechanisms of adaptation to a persistent stress factor can be detrimental under dynamically interacting conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that HOG pathway mutants, which are maladapted to constant osmotic stress, show better fitness under AS conditions.

claim: Microfluidics systems have been developed to study the frequency responses of cellular functions.
source: The development of microfluidics systems to study the frequency responses of cellular functions (Bennett and Hasty, 2009; Kaiser et al., 2018; Hersen et al., 2008; Mettetal et al., 2008) (e.g. signaling pathways, gene regulatory networks) has been instrumental in the adoption of the concepts of dynamic systems and information processing in biology.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work in the field.

claim: Changing the metabolic environment can profoundly affect cell physiology and alter stress responses.
source: For instance, changing the metabolic environment (e.g. carbon source type and concentration) can profoundly affect cell physiology (e.g. respiration and fermentation in yeast) and alter stress responses (Babazadeh et al., 2017; Rodaki et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Resource allocation is an important fundamental and applied topic in cell biology.
source: More generally, resource allocation (i.e. how cellular resources are shared between several cellular functions) is an important fundamental (Weiße et al., 2015; Metzl-Raz et al., 2017) (e.g. understanding growth laws) and applied topic (Ceroni et al., 2018) (e.g. design of robust synthetic gene circuits and bioproduction).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The trade-off between proliferation and stress responses can be an important determinant of cell fitness in a dynamic environment.
source: The trade-off between proliferation and stress responses can be an important determinant of cell fitness in a dynamic environment (Weiße et al., 2015; Metzl-Raz et al., 2017; Granados et al., 2017; Reimers et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The adaptation to hyperosmotic stress in Saccharomyces cerevisiae involves the HOG pathway.
source: The adaptation to hyperosmotic stress in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae involves an adaptive pathway—the HOG pathway—that has been extensively described at the molecular level (de Nadal and Posas, 2022) as well as biophysical and integrative levels through mathematical and computational models (Klipp et al., 2005; Muzzey et al., 2009; Petelenz-Kurdziel et al., 2013; Sharifian et al., 2015; Krantz et al., 2009; Zi et al., 2010; Schaber et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on the HOG pathway.

claim: Accumulation of intracellular glycerol is required to restore cellular osmotic balance when external osmolarity increases.
source: When external osmolarity increases, accumulation of intracellular glycerol is required to restore the cellular osmotic balance (Hohmann, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Osmotic stress signaling is orchestrated by a MAPK cascade culminating in double phosphorylation and nuclear accumulation of Hog1p.
source: At the molecular level, osmotic stress signaling is orchestrated by a mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascade, which culminates in double phosphorylation and nuclear accumulation of the MAPK protein Hog1p and differential regulation of hundreds of genes (Saito and Posas, 2012; Gasch et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GPD1 is upregulated after hyperosmotic stress.
source: In particular, GPD1 (NAD-dependent glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase), a key enzyme involved in the production of glycerol from glucose, is upregulated after hyperosmotic stress (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: Phosphorylated Hog1p triggers cell cycle arrest.
source: Phosphorylated Hog1p also triggers several processes in the cytoplasm that are essential for osmoregulation (Muzzey et al., 2009; Petelenz-Kurdziel et al., 2013), including cell cycle arrest (Escoté et al., 2004; Clotet et al., 2006; Duch et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The HOG pathway behaves as a low-pass filter that drives perfect adaptation.
source: Dynamically, the HOG pathway behaves as a low-pass filter that drives (perfect) adaptation through at least two layers of feedback loops that allow for deactivation of the pathway (Muzzey et al., 2009) (transcriptionally and within the cytoplasm).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The HOG pathway can be hyper-activated when stimulated at high frequencies, which drastically slows down the cell cycle.
source: Notably, the HOG pathway can be hyper-activated when stimulated at high frequencies, which drastically slows down the cell cycle (Mitchell et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Previous studies on the HOG pathway were carried out in a glucose-rich environment.
source: Although very informative—and an excellent example of how biological and physical concepts can be combined to obtain a comprehensive description of gene regulatory network dynamics—these studies were carried out in a glucose-rich environment, which insulates metabolic needs from osmotic stress adaptation requirements.
evidence: This is a statement about the conditions of previous studies.

claim: Glucose is needed for growth, production of glycerol, and the transcriptional feedback loop that deactivates the HOG pathway.
source: Glucose is not only needed for growth, but also for production of glycerol and the transcriptional feedback loop that deactivates the HOG pathway (Babazadeh et al., 2017; Muzzey et al., 2009); thus, cells may employ a decision mechanism to share glucose internally between these processes, particularly when glucose is scarce, or its availability fluctuates.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and leads to a hypothesis about glucose allocation.

claim: The average division rate strongly decreased as the frequency of osmotic shock increased.
source: The average division rate strongly decreased as the frequency of osmotic shock increased (Figure 2a), both in 2% glucose (2.2-fold reduction of division rate between periods of fluctuation T=192 min and T=12 min) and in 0.1% glucose (3.8-fold reduction of division rate between periods of fluctuation T=192 min and T=12 min).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The division rate was reduced 2.2-fold in 2% glucose between periods of fluctuation T=192 min and T=12 min.
source: The average division rate strongly decreased as the frequency of osmotic shock increased (Figure 2a), both in 2% glucose (2.2-fold reduction of division rate between periods of fluctuation T=192 min and T=12 min) and in 0.1% glucose (3.8-fold reduction of division rate between periods of fluctuation T=192 min and T=12 min).
evidence: This specific quantitative result is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2a.

claim: The division rate was reduced 3.8-fold in 0.1% glucose between periods of fluctuation T=192 min and T=12 min.
source: The average division rate strongly decreased as the frequency of osmotic shock increased (Figure 2a), both in 2% glucose (2.2-fold reduction of division rate between periods of fluctuation T=192 min and T=12 min) and in 0.1% glucose (3.8-fold reduction of division rate between periods of fluctuation T=192 min and T=12 min).
evidence: This specific quantitative result is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2a.

claim: The results are consistent with findings from Mitchell et al., 2015, who attributed the drastic decrease in cellular growth at high frequency of osmotic shocks to overactivation of the HOG pathway.
source: These results are consistent with findings from Mitchell et al., 2015, who attributed the drastic decrease in cellular growth observed at high frequency of osmotic shocks to overactivation of the HOG pathway.
evidence: This statement compares the current results to previous work.

claim: A clear negative relationship between the frequency of hyperosmotic stress and the division rate was observed in HOG pathway mutants.
source: However, we also observed a clear negative relationship between the frequency of hyperosmotic stress and the division rate of HOG pathway mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), indicating that the growth slowdown was not only explained by overactivation of the HOG pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The growth slowdown at high frequency of osmotic stress was not only explained by overactivation of the HOG pathway.
source: However, we also observed a clear negative relationship between the frequency of hyperosmotic stress and the division rate of HOG pathway mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), indicating that the growth slowdown was not only explained by overactivation of the HOG pathway.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation that HOG mutants also show frequency-dependent growth slowdown.

claim: Yeast cells are more sensitive to repeated than persistent hyperosmotic stress.
source: This negative relationship and the fact that cellular growth can rapidly recover after exposure to high osmolarity (Figure 2e–f) both indicate that yeast cells are more sensitive to repeated than persistent hyperosmotic stress.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the frequency-dependent division rate and recovery dynamics shown in Figure 2.

claim: A positive relationship was observed between the frequency of glucose availability and division rate in 2% glucose.
source: In contrast to the negative effect of osmotic stress frequency, we observed a positive relationship between the frequency of glucose availability and division rate (Figure 2b): cells divided faster when glucose availability fluctuated rapidly (0.0051 division/min at a fluctuation period T=12 min, corresponding to a doubling time of 136 min) than slowly (0.0027 division/min at a fluctuation period T=192 min, corresponding to a doubling time of 257 min).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Cells divided at 0.0051 division/min at a glucose fluctuation period T=12 min, corresponding to a doubling time of 136 min.
source: In contrast to the negative effect of osmotic stress frequency, we observed a positive relationship between the frequency of glucose availability and division rate (Figure 2b): cells divided faster when glucose availability fluctuated rapidly (0.0051 division/min at a fluctuation period T=12 min, corresponding to a doubling time of 136 min) than slowly (0.0027 division/min at a fluctuation period T=192 min, corresponding to a doubling time of 257 min).
evidence: This specific quantitative result is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2b.

claim: Cells divided at 0.0027 division/min at a glucose fluctuation period T=192 min, corresponding to a doubling time of 257 min.
source: In contrast to the negative effect of osmotic stress frequency, we observed a positive relationship between the frequency of glucose availability and division rate (Figure 2b): cells divided faster when glucose availability fluctuated rapidly (0.0051 division/min at a fluctuation period T=12 min, corresponding to a doubling time of 136 min) than slowly (0.0027 division/min at a fluctuation period T=192 min, corresponding to a doubling time of 257 min).
evidence: This specific quantitative result is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2b.

claim: The frequency of glucose availability did not significantly impact the division rate in 0.1% glucose.
source: However, this behavior was only observed in 2% glucose: the frequency of glucose availability did not significantly impact the division rate in 0.1% glucose (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The division rate was lower during half-periods without glucose than during half-periods with glucose under periodic fluctuations of 2% glucose.
source: Under periodic fluctuations of 2% glucose, the division rate was lower during half-periods without glucose than during half-periods with glucose (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), as expected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The average division rate during half-periods without glucose was higher at high frequency than at low frequency of glucose fluctuations.
source: However, this difference depended on the frequency of glucose fluctuations: the average division rate during half-periods without glucose was higher at high frequency (small period) than at low frequency (large period) of fluctuations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The effect of the frequency of glucose availability on the division rate in 2% glucose is likely due to a delay between glucose removal and growth arrest.
source: Therefore, the effect of the frequency of glucose availability on the division rate in 2% glucose is likely due to a delay between glucose removal and growth arrest: cell proliferation never stops when the frequency of glucose depletion is too fast.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the observation that division rate depends on frequency of glucose fluctuations.

claim: Cells behave as a low-pass filter for osmotic stress with respect to their division rate.
source: Therefore, with respect to their division rate, cells behave as a low-pass filter for osmotic stress but as a high-pass filter for glucose fluctuations.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the frequency-dependent division rate patterns observed for osmotic stress and glucose.

claim: Cells behave as a high-pass filter for glucose fluctuations with respect to their division rate.
source: Therefore, with respect to their division rate, cells behave as a low-pass filter for osmotic stress but as a high-pass filter for glucose fluctuations.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the frequency-dependent division rate patterns observed for osmotic stress and glucose.

claim: The division rate is similar when the frequencies of glucose availability and sorbitol exposure are both equal to 0.039 min–1, corresponding to a period of 26 min and a division rate of 0.004 division/min.
source: Moreover, the division rate is similar when the frequencies of glucose availability and sorbitol exposure are both equal to 0.039 min–1 (intersection of the two curves on Figure 2c), corresponding to a period of 26 min and a division rate of 0.004 division/min.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Under both IPS and AS conditions with a period of 24 min, the division rate was more than twofold lower than under periodic fluctuations of only glucose or sorbitol.
source: Under both IPS and AS conditions, the division rate was more than twofold lower than under periodic fluctuations of only glucose or sorbitol (Figure 3a), showing that dual environmental fluctuations have a non-additive, synergistic impact on cell growth.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Dual environmental fluctuations have a non-additive, synergistic impact on cell growth.
source: Under both IPS and AS conditions, the division rate was more than twofold lower than under periodic fluctuations of only glucose or sorbitol (Figure 3a), showing that dual environmental fluctuations have a non-additive, synergistic impact on cell growth.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation that the combined effect is greater than expected from individual effects.

claim: Cells divided about twice as fast under IPS condition (1.67×10–3 division/min) than under AS condition (9.4×10–4 division/min) when the fluctuation period was 24 min.
source: Strikingly, cells divided about twice as fast under IPS condition (1.67×10–3 division/min, corresponding to an average doubling time of 415 min) than under AS condition (9.4×10–4 division/min, corresponding to an average doubling time of 737 min) when the fluctuation period was 24 min (t-test, p=1.35 × 10–5; Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b)
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The difference in division rate between IPS and AS at period 24 min was statistically significant (p=1.35 × 10–5).
source: Strikingly, cells divided about twice as fast under IPS condition (1.67×10–3 division/min, corresponding to an average doubling time of 415 min) than under AS condition (9.4×10–4 division/min, corresponding to an average doubling time of 737 min) when the fluctuation period was 24 min (t-test, p=1.35 × 10–5; Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b)
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the text.

claim: At a fluctuation period of 96 min, cells divided faster under IPS (2.98×10–3 division/min) than under AS (1.83×10–3 division/min) with p=4.10 × 10–5.
source: or 96 min (2.98×10–3 division/min in IPS vs 1.83×10–3 division/min in AS; p=4.10 × 10–5; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: A similar pattern of faster growth under IPS than AS was observed when using 0.1% glucose instead of 2% glucose for both 24 min and 96 min fluctuation periods.
source: A similar pattern of faster growth was observed under IPS and AS conditions when we used 0.1% glucose instead of 2% glucose, for both a fluctuation period of 24 min (0.84×10–3 division/min under IPS vs 0.54×10–3 division/min under AS; t-test, p=8.03 × 10–5; Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) and 96 min (2.24×10–3 division/min under IPS vs 1.17×10–3 division/min under AS; t-test, p=6.80 × 10–3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: Under IPS condition with 96 min period, the division rate quickly increased to 4.86×10–3 division/min during the half-period with 2% glucose.
source: Under IPS condition, the division rate fluctuated largely over time: after the transition to 2% glucose, the division rate quickly increased to reach a plateau (4.86×10–3 division/min on average during the half-period with 2% glucose); after the transition to 1 M sorbitol in the absence of glucose, cell division was greatly slowed down (1.34×10–3 division/min during the half-period without glucose).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Under IPS condition with 96 min period, cell division was greatly slowed down to 1.34×10–3 division/min during the half-period without glucose.
source: Under IPS condition, the division rate fluctuated largely over time: after the transition to 2% glucose, the division rate quickly increased to reach a plateau (4.86×10–3 division/min on average during the half-period with 2% glucose); after the transition to 1 M sorbitol in the absence of glucose, cell division was greatly slowed down (1.34×10–3 division/min during the half-period without glucose).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Under AS condition with 96 min period, the division rate remained much more constant over time with 1.69×10–3 division/min during the half-period with 2% glucose and sorbitol and 1.89×10–3 division/min during the half-period without glucose and sorbitol.
source: In contrast, the division rate remained much more constant over time under AS condition: the average division rate was 1.69×10–3 division/min during the half-period with 2% glucose and 1 M sorbitol and 1.89×10–3 division/min during the half-period without glucose and sorbitol.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Cells appear to use glucose more efficiently for growth under IPS than AS conditions.
source: Therefore, cells appear to use glucose more efficiently for growth under IPS than AS conditions.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation that cells divide faster under IPS despite the same glucose availability.

claim: The slower cell division rate under AS compared to IPS could be explained by the allocation of intracellular glucose to the osmotic stress response under AS when cells are exposed to glucose and sorbitol simultaneously.
source: The slower cell division rate observed under AS when compared to IPS could be explained by the allocation of intracellular glucose to the osmotic stress response under AS when cells are exposed to glucose and sorbitol simultaneously, leaving less glucose available for growth.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed difference in division rates.

claim: In response to hyperosmotic stress, glycerol is synthesized from DHAP derived from glucose.
source: Indeed, in response to hyperosmotic stress glycerol is synthesized from a glycolysis intermediate (DHAP) derived from glucose (Norbeck et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The division rate was significantly lower under AS than IPS for almost all mutants (hog1Δ, pbs2Δ, gpd1Δ, gpd2Δ, gpd1Δ; gpd2Δ and fps1Δ) at a fluctuation period of 24 min with 2% glucose.
source: At a fluctuation period of 24 min, the division rate was significantly lower under AS than IPS for almost all mutants (hog1Δ, pbs2Δ, gpd1Δ, gpd2Δ, gpd1Δ; gpd2Δ and fps1Δ) both with fluctuations of 2% glucose (Figure 4a) and 0.1% glucose (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The ste11Δ mutant exhibited similar division rates under AS and IPS at a fluctuation period of 24 min.
source: However, the ste11Δ mutant exhibited similar division rates under AS and IPS (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: At a fluctuation period of 96 min, the division rates of ste11Δ and pbs2Δ mutants were significantly lower under AS than IPS.
source: At a fluctuation period of 96 min, the division rates of the two mutants we tested, ste11Δ and pbs2Δ, were significantly lower under AS than IPS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and c.

claim: Mutations known to reduce intracellular accumulation of glycerol did not attenuate the growth differences observed between IPS and AS conditions.
source: In conclusion, mutations known to reduce intracellular accumulation of glycerol did not attenuate the growth differences that we observed in the wild-type strain between IPS and AS conditions.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the mutant analysis showing similar IPS vs AS differences as wild-type.

claim: Allocation of glucose toward glycerol synthesis during hyperosmotic stress is not responsible for the lower division rate observed under AS than IPS.
source: Therefore, allocation of glucose toward glycerol synthesis during hyperosmotic stress is not responsible for the lower division rate observed under AS than IPS.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the mutant analysis.

claim: Glucose starvation was previously shown to induce fast inhibition of transcription.
source: Glucose starvation was previously shown to induce fast inhibition of transcription (Jona et al., 2000) and translation initiation (Ashe et al., 2000; Joyner et al., 2016), leading to cell growth reduction.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A significant reduction of division rate under AS relative to IPS was observed when using galactose as a carbon source.
source: We observed a significant reduction of division rate under AS condition relative to IPS condition when using galactose as a carbon source, similar to what we observed in glucose (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fast inhibition of transcription and translation occurring after glucose starvation but not after galactose starvation does not contribute significantly to the slower growth in AS condition.
source: Therefore, fast inhibition of transcription and translation occurring after glucose starvation but not after galactose starvation does not contribute significantly to the slower growth in AS condition.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation that galactose shows similar IPS vs AS differences as glucose.

claim: Yeast cells accumulate carbohydrate reserves such as glycogen to cope with nutrient starvation.
source: Yeast cells accumulate carbohydrate reserves such as glycogen to cope with nutrient starvation (Wilson et al., 2010; François and Parrou, 2001), and this reserve of glycogen can be mobilized during hyperosmotic stress (Bonny et al., 2021; Parrou et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Glycogen storage was not significantly contributing to the difference in division rates between AS and IPS conditions.
source: Once again, we observed a significantly lower division rate of glc3Δ cells in AS condition relative to IPS condition similar to what was observed in wild-type cells, suggesting that glycogen storage was not significantly contributing to this difference.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation that glc3Δ mutant shows similar IPS vs AS differences as wild-type.

claim: In response to hyperosmotic shock, residue 173 of Sic1p is phosphorylated by Hog1p, resulting in Sic1p stabilization and cell cycle arrest at the G1 phase.
source: In response to hyperosmotic shock, residue 173 of Sic1p is phosphorylated by Hog1p, resulting in Sic1p stabilization and cell cycle arrest at the G1 phase (Escoté et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: sic1(T173A) and sic1(T172E) mutant cells showed a similar decrease of division rate in AS relative to IPS as observed in wild-type cells.
source: However, sic1(T173A) mutant cells (unphosphorylatable Sic1p) and sic1(T172E) mutant cells (constitutive Sic1p stabilization) showed a similar decrease of division rate in AS condition relative to IPS condition as observed in wild-type cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The mechanism(s) responsible for the lower division rate in AS condition relative to IPS condition remain(s) elusive.
source: The mechanism(s) responsible for the lower division rate in AS condition relative to IPS condition therefore remain(s) elusive.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging that the mechanism is not yet understood despite testing multiple hypotheses.

claim: A high proportion of wild-type cells died under AS.
source: We noticed a high proportion of wild-type cells dying under AS (Figure 5a): some cells suddenly burst with their nucleus staying in the growth chamber, others became opaque and stopped growing with their nucleus remaining completely still (the nucleus of living cells wobbled over time).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Death events mostly occurred within minutes of the transition from medium containing 2% glucose and 1 M sorbitol to medium without glucose and sorbitol.
source: These death events mostly occurred within minutes of the transition from medium containing 2% glucose and 1 M sorbitol to medium without glucose and sorbitol (Figure 5—figure supplement 1d), suggesting cell lysis occurred due to hypo-osmotic shock following removal of 1 M sorbitol.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Cell lysis occurred due to hypo-osmotic shock following removal of 1 M sorbitol.
source: These death events mostly occurred within minutes of the transition from medium containing 2% glucose and 1 M sorbitol to medium without glucose and sorbitol (Figure 5—figure supplement 1d), suggesting cell lysis occurred due to hypo-osmotic shock following removal of 1 M sorbitol.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the timing of death events.

claim: Cell death was less frequent under IPS than AS conditions for the wild-type strain.
source: Cell death was less frequent under IPS than AS conditions for the wild-type strain (Figure 5a–c), even though the frequency of hypo-osmotic shock was the same in the two conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a-c.

claim: Lower intracellular accumulation of glycerol under IPS could be due to hyperosmotic stress being applied in the absence of glucose.
source: We reasoned this could be due to lower intracellular accumulation of glycerol under IPS, when hyperosmotic stress is applied in the absence of glucose.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the difference in death rates.

claim: Under AS, the presence of glucose during hyperosmotic stress could lead to faster intracellular accumulation of glycerol, resulting in stronger hypo-osmotic shock and cell lysis when sorbitol concentration suddenly drops.
source: Under AS, the presence of glucose during hyperosmotic stress could lead to faster intracellular accumulation of glycerol, resulting in stronger hypo-osmotic shock and cell lysis when the sorbitol concentration suddenly drops.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the higher death rate under AS.

claim: Significantly lower rates of cell death were observed for all mutants tested (ste11Δ, hog1Δ, pbs2Δ, gpd1Δ, gpd2Δ and gpd1Δ; gpd2Δ) relative to wild-type under AS but not under IPS.
source: Indeed, we observed significantly lower rates of cell death for all mutants tested (ste11Δ, hog1Δ, pbs2Δ, gpd1Δ, gpd2Δ and gpd1Δ; gpd2Δ) relative to the wild-type strain under AS, but not under IPS for which glycerol synthesis is frustrated even in wild-type cells due to the absence of glucose during hyperosmotic stress (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The death rate decreased from 2.4×10–3 min–1 for wild-type to 5.2×10–5, 3.4×10–4, and 3.5×10–4 min–1 for hog1Δ, pbs2Δ, and gpd1Δ; gpd2Δ mutants respectively under AS when the fluctuation period was 24 min.
source: In particular, the death rate decreased from 2.4×10–3 min–1 for wild-type to 5.2×10–5, 3.4×10–4, and 3.5×10–4 min–1, respectively, for the hog1Δ, pbs2Δ, and gpd1Δ; gpd2Δ mutants under AS when the fluctuation period was 24 min.
evidence: This specific quantitative result is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5c.

claim: A higher death rate was observed for the fps1Δ mutant (3.5×10–3 min–1) under AS.
source: Conversely, we observed a higher death rate for the fps1Δ mutant (3.5×10–3 min–1) under AS (Figure 5c), which is consistent with higher intracellular accumulation of glycerol in this mutant lacking the Fps1 aquaglyceroporin channel involved in glycerol export.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The higher death rate of fps1Δ mutant is consistent with higher intracellular accumulation of glycerol in this mutant lacking the Fps1 aquaglyceroporin channel involved in glycerol export.
source: Conversely, we observed a higher death rate for the fps1Δ mutant (3.5×10–3 min–1) under AS (Figure 5c), which is consistent with higher intracellular accumulation of glycerol in this mutant lacking the Fps1 aquaglyceroporin channel involved in glycerol export.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed death rate to known function of Fps1.

claim: Over a 10 hr AS experiment with a fluctuation period of 24 min, the death rate was lowest at the beginning and maximal during the last 5 hr.
source: Over a 10 hr AS experiment with a fluctuation period of 24 min, the death rate was lowest at the beginning of the experiment and was maximal during the last 5 hr of the experiment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1e.

claim: When the AS fluctuation period was 96 min, the maximum death rate occurred earlier and the dynamics of cell death remained constant over multiple periods of osmotic fluctuation.
source: However, when the AS fluctuation period was 96 min, the maximum death rate occurred earlier (and stopped increasing after the second period) and the dynamics of cell death remained constant over multiple periods of osmotic fluctuation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1f.

claim: The observations of death rate dynamics are consistent with cell death being due to glycerol accumulation.
source: Again, these observations are consistent with cell death being due to glycerol accumulation, since it takes time for cells to accumulate an amount of glycerol sufficient to cause bursting after hypo-osmotic shock.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the temporal dynamics of death to glycerol accumulation.

claim: Under IPS, the population growth rates of most mutant strains and of the wild-type strain were not significantly different, with the exception of the slightly lower growth rate of the ste11Δ mutant.
source: Under IPS, the population growth rates of most mutant strains and of the wild-type strain were not significantly different; the only exception being the slightly lower growth rate of the ste11Δ mutant (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Under AS with a fluctuation period of 24 min, several mutants had higher population growth rates than the wild-type strain.
source: However, under AS with a fluctuation period of 24 min, several mutants had higher population growth rates than the wild-type strain (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The population growth rate was negative for the wild-type strain (–1.4×10–3 min–1) and positive for the hog1Δ mutant (1.0×10–3 min–1) and pbs2Δ mutant (5.5×10–4 min–1) under AS with a fluctuation period of 24 min.
source: In fact, the population growth rate was negative for the wild-type strain (–1.4×10–3 min–1) as cells died faster than they divided and positive for the hog1Δ mutant (1.0×10–3 min–1) and pbs2Δ mutant (5.5×10–4 min–1).
evidence: This specific quantitative result is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5d.

claim: The hog1Δ and pbs2Δ genotypes are better adapted and would quickly outcompete wild-type cells under AS conditions with a fluctuation period of 24 min.
source: Thus, the hog1Δ and pbs2Δ genotypes are better adapted and would quickly outcompete wild-type cells under these dynamic conditions.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the higher population growth rates of these mutants compared to wild-type.

claim: No significant differences in population growth rate were observed between wild-type and pbs2Δ mutant under AS when the fluctuation period was 96 min.
source: However, this is only true when the frequency of environmental fluctuations is sufficiently high, since we did not observe significant differences in the population growth rate between the wild-type and pbs2Δ mutant under AS when the fluctuation period was 96 min (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Mutants that were characterized by an inability to adapt to prolonged hyperosmotic stress can be well adapted when hyperosmotic stress rapidly fluctuates in antiphase with glucose availability.
source: We conclude that mutants that were first characterized by an inability to adapt to prolonged hyperosmotic stress can be well adapted when hyperosmotic stress rapidly fluctuates in antiphase with glucose availability.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the fitness advantage of HOG mutants under fast AS conditions.

claim: The genetic mechanisms that contribute to adaptation under steady-state conditions could be detrimental under dynamic conditions.
source: Therefore, the genetic mechanisms that contribute to adaptation under steady-state conditions could be detrimental under dynamic conditions, highlighting the importance of investigating how organisms adapt to dynamically changing environments.
evidence: This is a general conclusion inferred from the observation that wild-type is less fit than mutants under certain dynamic conditions.

claim: No enrichment of Hog1-GFP in nuclei was detected when only glucose fluctuated over time.
source: We did not detect any enrichment of Hog1-GFP in nuclei when only glucose fluctuated over time (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), suggesting cells did not perceive glucose fluctuations as a significant osmotic cue.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Cells did not perceive glucose fluctuations as a significant osmotic cue.
source: We did not detect any enrichment of Hog1-GFP in nuclei when only glucose fluctuated over time (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), suggesting cells did not perceive glucose fluctuations as a significant osmotic cue.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of Hog1-GFP nuclear enrichment during glucose fluctuations.

claim: Previous studies observed small transient (<2 min) peaks of Hog1-GFP nuclear localization after glucose was added back following glucose depletion.
source: Although previous studies observed small transient (<2 min) peaks of Hog1-GFP nuclear localization after glucose was added back to the medium following glucose depletion (Sharifian et al., 2015; Piao et al., 2012), the temporal resolution in our experiments (one image every 6 min) may have been too low to detect these peaks.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work and explains why the current study may not have detected these peaks.

claim: Enrichment of Hog1-GFP fluorescence in nuclei was observed within minutes after exposure to 1 M sorbitol under both AS and IPS.
source: In contrast, enrichment of Hog1-GFP fluorescence in nuclei was observed within minutes after exposure to 1 M sorbitol under both AS (Figure 6a) and IPS (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a and 6b.

claim: Cells can sense hyperosmotic shock, activate the HOG MAPK cascade, and phosphorylate Hog1 MAP kinase both in the presence (AS) and absence (IPS) of glucose.
source: Therefore, cells can sense hyperosmotic shock, activate the HOG MAPK cascade, and phosphorylate Hog1 MAP kinase both in the presence (AS) and absence (IPS) of glucose.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation of Hog1-GFP nuclear enrichment under both conditions.

claim: The adaptation dynamics of Hog1p were remarkably different between AS and IPS conditions.
source: However, the adaptation dynamics of Hog1p (i.e. its exit from the nucleus) were remarkably different (Figure 6a–c): under AS, nuclear enrichment of Hog1-GFP peaked at 6 min following hyperosmotic shock and then quickly decayed and became undetectable after 30 min (Figure 6a and c)—essentially the same dynamics observed under periodic fluctuations of osmotic stress without glucose fluctuations (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a-c.

claim: Under AS, nuclear enrichment of Hog1-GFP peaked at 6 min following hyperosmotic shock and became undetectable after 30 min.
source: However, the adaptation dynamics of Hog1p (i.e. its exit from the nucleus) were remarkably different (Figure 6a–c): under AS, nuclear enrichment of Hog1-GFP peaked at 6 min following hyperosmotic shock and then quickly decayed and became undetectable after 30 min (Figure 6a and c)—essentially the same dynamics observed under periodic fluctuations of osmotic stress without glucose fluctuations (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a and 6c.

claim: Under IPS, nuclear enrichment of Hog1-GFP peaked 6 min after hyperosmotic shock, but Hog1-GFP returned to the cytosol much more slowly, with strong nuclear enrichment still observed 48 min after exposure to hyperosmotic stress in the absence of glucose.
source: Under IPS conditions, nuclear enrichment also peaked 6 min after hyperosmotic shock, but Hog1-GFP returned to the cytosol much more slowly; strong nuclear enrichment was still observed 48 min after exposure to hyperosmotic stress in the absence of glucose (Figure 6b and c).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b and 6c.

claim: When hyperosmotic stress was released under IPS, Hog1-GFP returned to the cytosol in less than 12 min.
source: When the hyperosmotic stress was released, Hog1-GFP returned to the cytosol in less than 12 min.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6.

claim: Nuclear enrichment of Hog1-GFP reached basal levels about 2 hr after the onset of hyperosmotic stress during a single pulse of 1 M sorbitol without glucose for 4 hr.
source: To determine whether Hog1-GFP eventually returns to the cytoplasm during hyperosmotic stress in the absence of glucose, we applied a single pulse of 1 M sorbitol without glucose for 4 hr. Nuclear enrichment of Hog1-GFP reached basal levels about 2 hr after the onset of hyperosmotic stress (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The delayed exit of Hog1-GFP out of the nucleus under IPS suggests that the activity of the feedback loop regulating Hog1p dephosphorylation is impaired in the absence of glucose.
source: The delayed exit of Hog1-GFP out of the nucleus under IPS suggests that the activity of the feedback loop regulating Hog1p dephosphorylation is impaired in the absence of glucose.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the observation of delayed Hog1-GFP nuclear export under IPS.

claim: Delayed nuclear export of Hog1-GFP under IPS could be due to impaired osmoregulation.
source: We hypothesized that delayed nuclear export of Hog1-GFP under IPS could be due to impaired osmoregulation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the delayed Hog1-GFP export.

claim: No recovery of cell size was observed during hyperosmotic stress under IPS conditions.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we observed no recovery of cell size during hyperosmotic stress under IPS conditions (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Under IPS, cells only returned to their initial size when sorbitol was removed and glucose was added back to the medium, which also corresponded to the moment when Hog1-GFP returned to the cytosol.
source: Cells only returned to their initial size when sorbitol was removed and glucose was added back to the medium, which also corresponded to the moment when Hog1-GFP returned to the cytosol.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6.

claim: Under AS, both the recovery of cell size and nuclear export of Hog1-GFP occurred while cells were still exposed to hyperosmotic stress.
source: In contrast, under AS, both the recovery of cell size and nuclear export of Hog1-GFP occurred while cells were still exposed to hyperosmotic stress (Figure 6), showing that osmoregulation was not impaired under these conditions.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Osmoregulation was not impaired under AS conditions.
source: In contrast, under AS, both the recovery of cell size and nuclear export of Hog1-GFP occurred while cells were still exposed to hyperosmotic stress (Figure 6), showing that osmoregulation was not impaired under these conditions.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation of cell size recovery and Hog1-GFP export during osmotic stress under AS.

claim: Glucose is necessary for the rapid osmoregulation that usually occurs in the first 20 min following hyperosmotic stress.
source: These results suggest glucose is necessary for the rapid osmoregulation that usually occurs in the first 20 min following hyperosmotic stress.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the comparison of osmoregulation dynamics under IPS vs AS.

claim: Fast osmoregulation has been proposed to rely on the induction of glycerol synthesis via Hog1p-dependent post-translational mechanisms.
source: This fast osmoregulation has been proposed to rely on the induction of glycerol synthesis via Hog1p-dependent post-translational mechanisms (Schaber et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The absence of glucose may prevent glycerol synthesis and thereby fast osmoregulation.
source: Since glucose is a metabolic precursor of glycerol, the absence of glucose may prevent glycerol synthesis and thereby fast osmoregulation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the known metabolic relationship between glucose and glycerol.

claim: Fast periodic fluctuation of osmotic stress was previously shown to cause hyper-activation of the STL1 promoter regulated by Hog1p.
source: Fast periodic fluctuation of osmotic stress was previously shown to cause hyper-activation of the STL1 promoter (PSTL1) regulated by Hog1p (Mitchell et al., 2015), while glucose depletion is known to inhibit transcription (Jona et al., 2000) and translation initiation (Ashe et al., 2000; Janapala et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Glucose depletion is known to inhibit transcription and translation initiation.
source: Fast periodic fluctuation of osmotic stress was previously shown to cause hyper-activation of the STL1 promoter (PSTL1) regulated by Hog1p (Mitchell et al., 2015), while glucose depletion is known to inhibit transcription (Jona et al., 2000) and translation initiation (Ashe et al., 2000; Janapala et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Transient expression of PSTL1-mCitrine was observed in response to both short (48 min) and long (10 hr) pulses of 1 M sorbitol.
source: As expected, we observed transient expression of PSTL1-mCitrine in response to both short (48 min) and long (10 hr) pulses of 1 M sorbitol (Figure 7): the mean fluorescence level peaked at a 2.8-fold change 115 min after exposure to a short sorbitol pulse and 2.4-fold change 122 min after a long sorbitol pulse; then, fluorescence gradually returned to basal levels, even when osmotic stress was maintained.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The mean fluorescence level of PSTL1-mCitrine peaked at a 2.8-fold change 115 min after exposure to a short sorbitol pulse.
source: As expected, we observed transient expression of PSTL1-mCitrine in response to both short (48 min) and long (10 hr) pulses of 1 M sorbitol (Figure 7): the mean fluorescence level peaked at a 2.8-fold change 115 min after exposure to a short sorbitol pulse and 2.4-fold change 122 min after a long sorbitol pulse; then, fluorescence gradually returned to basal levels, even when osmotic stress was maintained.
evidence: This specific quantitative result is stated in the text and supported by Figure 7.

claim: The mean fluorescence level of PSTL1-mCitrine peaked at a 2.4-fold change 122 min after a long sorbitol pulse.
source: As expected, we observed transient expression of PSTL1-mCitrine in response to both short (48 min) and long (10 hr) pulses of 1 M sorbitol (Figure 7): the mean fluorescence level peaked at a 2.8-fold change 115 min after exposure to a short sorbitol pulse and 2.4-fold change 122 min after a long sorbitol pulse; then, fluorescence gradually returned to basal levels, even when osmotic stress was maintained.
evidence: This specific quantitative result is stated in the text and supported by Figure 7.

claim: The expression pattern of PSTL1-mCitrine is consistent with previous quantifications of PSTL1 transcriptional activity during hyperosmotic stress.
source: This expression pattern is consistent with previous quantifications of PSTL1 transcriptional activity during hyperosmotic stress (Wosika and Pelet, 2020; Ben Meriem et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement compares the current results to previous work.

claim: When hyperosmotic shocks were periodically applied for 48 min every 96 min, PSTL1-mCitrine expression constantly increased to reach 10.2-fold change after 11 hr.
source: When hyperosmotic shocks were periodically applied for 48 min every 96 min, PSTL1-mCitrine expression constantly increased to reach 10.2-fold change after 11 hr (Figure 7b), suggesting a lack of adaptation to repeated osmotic shocks.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The constant increase in PSTL1-mCitrine expression under repeated osmotic shocks suggests a lack of adaptation to repeated osmotic shocks.
source: When hyperosmotic shocks were periodically applied for 48 min every 96 min, PSTL1-mCitrine expression constantly increased to reach 10.2-fold change after 11 hr (Figure 7b), suggesting a lack of adaptation to repeated osmotic shocks.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the observation of continuously increasing expression.

claim: Hyper-activation of PSTL1-mCitrine transcription was observed under AS conditions where PSTL1-mCitrine expression reached a maximum of 4.1-fold change after 413 min and remained as high as 3.1-fold change after 11 hr under the AS regime with a fluctuation period of 96 min.
source: Interestingly, hyper-activation of PSTL1-mCitrine transcription was also observed under AS conditions where PSTL1-mCitrine expression reached a maximum of 4.1-fold change after 413 min and remained as high as 3.1-fold change after 11 hr under the AS regime with a fluctuation period of 96 min (Figure 7a and b).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7a and 7b.

claim: Much weaker and slower induction of PSTL1-mCitrine expression was observed under IPS with a maximal fold change of 0.7 after 11 hr of IPS with a fluctuation period of 96 min.
source: Conversely, we observed much weaker and slower induction of PSTL1-mCitrine expression under IPS: the maximal fold change was 0.7 after 11 hr of IPS with a fluctuation period of 96 min (Figure 7a and b).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7a and 7b.

claim: A similar pattern of faster, stronger induction of PSTL1-mCitrine under AS than IPS was observed when the fluctuation period was 24 min.
source: We observed a similar pattern (i.e. faster, stronger induction of PSTL1-mCitrine under AS than IPS) when the fluctuation period was 24 min (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: The STL1 promoter is not activated by hyperosmotic stress in the absence of glucose, despite nuclear translocation of the MAP kinase Hog1p.
source: Therefore, the STL1 promoter is not activated by hyperosmotic stress in the absence of glucose, despite nuclear translocation of the MAP kinase Hog1p.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the weak PSTL1-mCitrine expression under IPS despite Hog1p nuclear localization.

claim: The global repression of expression in response to abrupt glucose starvation is dominant over the hyper-activation of PSTL1 transcriptional activity induced by periodic osmotic stress.
source: This result suggests that the global repression of expression in response to abrupt glucose starvation is dominant over the hyper-activation of PSTL1 transcriptional activity induced by periodic osmotic stress.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the observation that PSTL1 is not activated under IPS.

claim: Dual fluctuations of glucose deprivation and osmotic stress had synergistic (non-additive) effects on cell proliferation that could not be easily predicted from the effects of fluctuating each stress separately.
source: We found that dual fluctuations of glucose deprivation and osmotic stress had synergistic (non-additive) effects on cell proliferation that could not be easily predicted from the effects of fluctuating each stress separately.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The phasing of the two stresses had a striking impact on several cell phenotypes, including division rate, death rate, osmoregulation, and transcriptional activation of a gene regulated by osmotic stress.
source: The phasing of the two stresses had a striking impact on several cell phenotypes, including division rate, death rate, osmoregulation, and transcriptional activation of a gene regulated by osmotic stress.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The classic picture of yeast adaptation to osmotic stress cannot fully explain the behavior of yeast cells under fluctuating conditions.
source: Moreover, our results indicate that the classic picture of yeast adaptation to osmotic stress cannot fully explain the behavior of yeast cells under fluctuating conditions.
evidence: This is a general conclusion inferred from the observation of glucose-dependent responses.

claim: While the HOG signaling pathway was activated under all conditions, transcription of the target genes and inactivation of the HOG pathway were only detected when glucose and hyperosmotic stress were applied simultaneously, but not when hyperosmotic stress occurred in the absence of glucose.
source: Indeed, by making glucose available for only short durations, we produced an environment in which the dynamics of the osmotic signaling pathway and its interaction with the glucose sensing pathway and glycolysis are critical. While the HOG signaling pathway was activated under all conditions, transcription of the target genes and inactivation of the HOG pathway were only detected when glucose and hyperosmotic stress were applied simultaneously, but not when hyperosmotic stress occurred in the absence of glucose.
evidence: This is a summary of the key findings regarding HOG pathway dynamics under different conditions.

claim: If glucose is not available in the environment, cells are unable to commit to classical transcriptional/translational responses after osmotic stress.
source: Therefore, if glucose is not available in the environment, cells are unable to commit to classical transcriptional/translational responses after osmotic stress.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the lack of PSTL1 activation under IPS.

claim: A recent study showed that yeast cells displayed a stronger response to hyperosmotic stress at lower glucose concentration, including higher expression of several genes regulated by the HOG pathway.
source: This finding may seem inconsistent with conclusions of a recent study showing that yeast cells displayed a stronger response to hyperosmotic stress at lower glucose concentration, including higher expression of several genes regulated by the HOG pathway (Shen et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Shen et al., 2023, investigated the response to a single hyperosmotic shock at diverse constant glucose concentrations, not dynamic stresses, and the lowest glucose concentration they considered was 0.02% allowing slow cell growth, not complete glucose depletion that stopped growth.
source: However, key differences in experimental procedures may explain this apparent discrepancy: Shen et al., 2023, investigated the response to a single hyperosmotic shock at diverse constant glucose concentrations—not dynamic stresses as we did—and the lowest glucose concentration they considered was 0.02% allowing slow cell growth—not complete glucose depletion that stopped growth.
evidence: This statement describes the experimental conditions of a previous study to explain differences in results.

claim: Subtle changes in the metabolic environment of cells may have profound impact on their stress-response capacity.
source: This further suggests that subtle changes in the metabolic environment of cells may have profound impact on their stress-response capacity.
evidence: This is a general conclusion inferred from the comparison with previous work.

claim: Another recent study showed that the interplay between osmotic stress and glucose concentration could cause bimodal expression of a key determinant of cell survival after starvation.
source: Interestingly, another recent study showed that the interplay between osmotic stress and glucose concentration could cause bimodal expression of a key determinant of cell survival after starvation (Lukačišin et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In contrast to the well-known proliferative defects of osmo-sensitive mutants under constant hyperosmotic conditions, periodically varying osmotic stress is not always detrimental to the growth of osmo-sensitive yeast cells.
source: Importantly, in contrast to the well-known proliferative defects of osmo-sensitive mutants under constant hyperosmotic conditions, we show that periodically varying osmotic stress is not always detrimental to the growth of osmo-sensitive yeast cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the mutant fitness results.

claim: HOG pathway mutants can grow and are even fitter than wild-type cells under fast alternating fluctuations of glucose deprivation and hyperosmotic stress.
source: Indeed, HOG pathway mutants can grow and are even fitter than wild-type cells under fast alternating fluctuations of glucose deprivation and hyperosmotic stress.
evidence: This is directly supported by population growth rate data.

claim: Osmo-sensitive mutant cells survive better than wild-type cells to repeated hypo-osmotic shocks under AS, probably because they do not accumulate glycerol in response to hyperosmotic shocks and thus are less sensitive to fluctuations in the osmolarity of their environment.
source: In this condition, osmo-sensitive mutant cells survive better than wild-type cells to repeated hypo-osmotic shocks, probably because they do not accumulate glycerol in response to hyperosmotic shocks and thus are less sensitive to fluctuations in the osmolarity of their environment.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the lower death rates of HOG mutants under AS.

claim: Cells can be killed by exploiting their adaptive response.
source: This also suggests that cells can be killed by exploiting their adaptive response.
evidence: This is a general conclusion inferred from the observation that wild-type cells die more under AS due to their glycerol accumulation response.

claim: Forcing cells to repeatedly express their osmoadaptation program makes them very sensitive to osmotic rupture of the cell wall.
source: Forcing cells to repeatedly express their osmoadaptation program makes them very sensitive to osmotic rupture of the cell wall.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the high death rate of wild-type cells under AS.

claim: Periodically stressing cells (and their metabolic state) may be an efficient strategy to kill yeast cells.
source: Hence, periodically stressing cells (and their metabolic state) may be an efficient strategy to kill yeast cells.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the observed death rates.

claim: Varying the timescale of fluctuations may prevent cells from finding an evolutionary escape route.
source: We further imagine that varying the timescale of fluctuations may even prevent cells from finding an evolutionary escape route.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: All S. cerevisiae strains used in this study are derived from BY4741 or BY4742.
source: All S. cerevisiae strains used in this study are derived from BY4741 or BY4742 (Brachmann et al., 1998) and are listed in Tables 1 and 2.
evidence: This is a statement about the materials used in the study.

claim: The reference strain yPH_132 expresses the mCherry fluorescent reporter fused to histone H2B to label cell nuclei.
source: The reference strain yPH_132 expresses the mCherry fluorescent reporter fused to histone H2B to label cell nuclei.
evidence: This is a description of the strain construction.

claim: Yeast cells were cultivated and imaged in custom-made microfluidic devices for all time-lapse microscopy experiments.
source: Yeast cells were cultivated and imaged in custom-made microfluidic devices for all time-lapse microscopy experiments described in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The microfluidic chip consists of five independent pairs of flow channels connected each to five growth chambers where yeast cells are constrained to proliferate in monolayer.
source: In brief, it consists of five independent pairs of flow channels (800 µm wide×50 µm high) connected each to five growth chambers (400×400×3.8 µm3; L×W×H) where yeast cells are constrained to proliferate in monolayer.
evidence: This is a description of the microfluidic device design.

claim: ilastik v1.3 was used for the segmentation and tracking of cell nuclei expressing HTB2-mCherry on fluorescence images.
source: We used ilastik v1.3 for the segmentation and tracking of cell nuclei expressing HTB2-mCherry on fluorescence images.
evidence: This is a description of the image analysis method.
